content: The World Health Organization (WHO) introduced updated guidelines in 2015 to standardize the monitoring and evaluation of HIV services at facility, subnational, and national levels. Six of these indicators rely on data derived from patient diagnosis, testing, and medical records. These six indicators include: (1) the proportion of individuals diagnosed with HIV, (2) linkage to care, (3) initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), (4) retention on ART, (5) viral load suppression, and (6) mortality. In 2017, WHO launched the Consolidated Guidelines on Person-Centered HIV Patient Monitoring and Case Surveillance. These guidelines aim to integrate routine patient monitoring, program monitoring, and surveillance into a unified monitoring and evaluation (M&E) system. This approach shifts the focus from counting services delivered to prioritizing people and their access to linked HIV and health services. The guidelines emphasize person-centered monitoring, HIV case surveillance, and the use of unique identifiers to track HIV services. A key recommendation is to conduct a comprehensive situational analysis as the first step in transitioning to person-centered HIV strategic information systems. The assessment tool for person-centered HIV patient monitoring and case surveillance provides a structured process for evaluating existing HIV strategic information systems, formats, and tools. It includes three main components: (1) a document review and information collection tool, (2) a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) analysis to identify priority actions, and (3) a scorecard and priority action plan summarizing key actions and resource requirements. Preliminary assessments conducted in various countries informed the adaptation of the 2017 WHO guidelines. The assessment tool evaluates several components, including the overall status of patient monitoring and case surveillance, opportunities for improvement, and recommendations for next steps. The process begins with a stakeholder meeting to review and adapt the data collection tool to the specific country context. In countries with established systems, the tool evaluates existing systems, while in others, it serves as a planning tool to define needs and guide the development of case surveillance and patient monitoring systems. The assessment involves a desk review of key documents, followed by interviews with stakeholders at national, subnational, and facility levels. Key stakeholders include representatives from the Ministry of Health, WHO, HIV program officers, monitoring and evaluation (M&E) officers, strategic information (SI) officers, technical working groups, and partner agencies such as the Global Fund and PEPFAR. The assessment aims to guide the implementation of 15 key recommendations from the guidelines, including transitioning to treat all, simplifying tools, improving data quality, integrating systems, and promoting the use of unique identifiers. The assessment also evaluates the availability and functionality of patient-level data collection systems, reporting processes, and policies for patient monitoring and case surveillance. It examines the developmental stage of data systems, the quality and completeness of data, and the use of electronic systems. Additionally, it reviews strategic plans for patient monitoring and disease notification, as well as the integration of HIV surveillance with other notifiable diseases. For case surveillance, the assessment examines the availability of key data points, such as HIV diagnosis dates, CD4 and viral load results, ART initiation dates, and mortality data. It also evaluates the use of vital registration systems, the confidentiality and security of data, and the interoperability of information systems. The assessment includes interviews with key informants to understand the current status of HIV surveillance, identify gaps, and develop prioritized action plans. The guidelines emphasize the importance of transitioning from paper-based to electronic systems, ensuring data security, and using individual-level data to improve programs and long-term health outcomes. The assessment tool provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating and strengthening HIV patient monitoring and case surveillance systems to support person-centered care and improve program outcomes.
